# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Critical Reading: Varga & Holm, Re-examination of the Halden Pilot

**Bottom line:** The first half of this comment is valuable. The attrition finding, the comparison of manager ratings with organisations' own records, and the use of actual hours all correct real problems in the Halden paper with real data. The conclusion is a different matter. The authors' own best estimate still shows a gain of about 11% in output per actual hour. Calling the gains "entirely an artifact" depends on a novelty argument built from two data points. It also passes over the one randomised result that bears most directly on that residual: the Varden case-processing stratum.

## The numbers mostly check out

- **Table 2 gains:**
  - 95.1 / 0.8 = +18.9% ✓
  - 98.4 / 0.859 = +14.6% ✓
  - 95.4 / 0.861 = +10.8% ✓
- **Hours ratios:**
  - 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859, a fall of 14.1% ✓
  - 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861, a fall of 13.9% ✓
- **Real revenue:** 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974, a fall of about 2.6% ✓
- **Manager vs records:** 98.9 − 95.1 = 3.8 points ✓

There are two numerical problems:

1. **The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** The schedule is 32 hours. Longer days of +0.7 hours across four days add 2.8 hours, and day-off work adds 1.6 hours. That gives about 36.4 hours, not the reported 34.6. The figures reconcile if the 0.7 is per week rather than per day: 32 + 0.3 (baseline overtime) + 0.7 + 1.6 = 34.6. This looks like a typo, but as printed the breakdown contradicts the headline hours figure.
2. **The extrapolation date is wrong.** A straight line from 0.61 SD at month 3 to 0.29 SD at month 6 falls by about 0.107 SD per month. It reaches zero at about **month 8.7**, not "around month ten." The error matters for the argument in section 6 below.

## What the comment gets right

### 1. Attrition: a serious correction to the Halden paper

Halden said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." The microdata show otherwise:

- Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had started.
- Six of the nine cited workload or inability to maintain output.

This is a misstatement in the original paper, not just a limitation. It also makes the earlier survivorship concern much stronger.

### 2. The output measure

Managers' ratings were higher than their own records in 19 of 23 organisations, by 3.8 points on average. That is a systematic gap, and the authors present it fairly, without implying bad faith.

### 3. Actual hours

Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. This closely matches Varden, where actual hours fell 13% in case-processing offices, so the correction looks robust.

### 4. Revenue and sectors

The inflation adjustment is correct. The point that sector-level gains are "an artifact of the per-hour metric" is right; I made the same point about the original paper.

## Where the comment overreaches

### 1. The conclusion contradicts the comment's own estimate

After every correction the authors can make, the gain is still +10.8% in output per actual hour. Moving from "falls from 23% to 11%" to "entirely an artifact" needs the novelty argument to explain the whole remaining 11%. That argument rests on:

- **Two survey points.** A straight line fitted through two points can't distinguish a decline to zero from a decline to a plateau.
- **Energy, not output.** The survey measured self-reported energy, not productivity. The comment never shows that energy and output moved together.

The Data Note concedes that the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the conclusion goes further than the whole pilot: it covers "reduced-hours schemes" generally.

### 2. It cites Varden selectively

The comment calls Varden's counter-office result "the most reliable finding in the literature." It does not mention the case-processing result from the same randomised trial. That result has none of the problems the comment identifies in Halden:

| Problem in Halden | Varden case-processing |
|---|---|
| Self-selection and attrition | Randomised by office |
| Manager-rated output | Administrative records |
| Scheduled hours | Timesheet hours |
| **Result** | **+12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4) at month 9** |

Month 9 is after the comment's own extrapolated point at which the novelty effect should have disappeared. The randomised evidence doesn't rule out novelty over a longer period. But it shows that selection and measurement problems cannot be the whole story, and it puts real pressure on the specific novelty timeline the comment proposes.

The two studies agree with each other: about +11% in the corrected Halden subset and +12.5% in Varden. A careful reader would treat that agreement as a finding, not ignore it.

### 3. It mischaracterises the meetings analysis

Some of the criticism is fair: the analysis was unregistered and uses n = 7. But two claims are inaccurate:

- **"A subgroup selected for analysis after the results were known."** The seven offices were all of the treated case-processing offices. No subgroup was picked out. Varden says the data were collected in month six at managers' request. What was unregistered was the measure, not the choice of offices.
- **"Should not be cited as a mechanism."** Varden never claimed it as an established mechanism. The authors said explicitly that the analysis "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test.

The comment also misses something that cuts against its own thesis. If cutting meetings explains much of the gain, the gain is real and durable rather than a novelty effect. It just isn't caused by rest. Halden's interview data, with meetings mentioned by 47 of 58 managers, point the same way.

### 4. The burden-of-proof standard is applied unevenly

The comment says the burden of proof lies with anyone claiming a durable effect. That is reasonable. But "entirely an artifact … of novelty" is also a positive claim, and the comment supports it with nothing beyond the energy extrapolation.

### 5. The abstract claims a correction the analysis doesn't make

The abstract says the authors corrected "the first three" problems: attrition, output measure and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is described but never quantified or bounded. Some form of bounding analysis, such as assigning plausible output levels to the nine organisations that withdrew, would show how much attrition could change the 10.8%. As written, it is unclear whether attrition explains a lot or a little.

### 6. Table 2 mixes samples

The first row covers all 61 organisations; the others cover subsets of 23, 27 and 17. Part of the fall from 23.4% to 10.8% may come from differences in which organisations are included rather than from the corrections. The clean comparison is to show the as-reported figure for the same 17 organisations. There are also no confidence intervals, so we can't tell whether the 10.8% is precisely estimated.

### 7. Smaller points

- The retail figure of −11.2% comes from three organisations.
- Some of the "records," such as billable hours delivered, partly measure input rather than output. That makes them awkward to use in a study about reducing hours.

## Synthesis across the three documents

| | Output per employee | Output per actual hour |
|---|---|---|
| Halden as reported | −1.3% | +23.4% (scheduled hours) |
| Halden corrected (17-organisation subset) | −4.6% | +10.8% |
| Varden case-processing (randomised) | −2.1% (CI −6.8 to +2.6) | +12.5% |
| Varden counter / contact centre (randomised) | −11.4% | +6.7% (largely higher utilisation) |

The best-supported reading is this:

- **Work not tied to presence.** A 20% cut in scheduled hours leads to a 13–14% cut in actual hours and a small loss of output per employee, roughly 2–5%. Output per actual hour rises by about 10–13%. Whether that gain lasts, and how much of it comes from cutting low-value time like meetings rather than from rest, is still open.
- **Work tied to presence.** Output and service fall.

This is much weaker than Halden's original claims. It is also not the "entirely an artifact" conclusion of this comment. The comment's methodological recommendations are sound: record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, longer follow-up, and intention-to-treat analysis. Its own conclusion should follow the same standard.
